chapter: Hampton and Basie: tours and road life
title: Basie on the bus; the 1950s before things improved
summary: Basie sometimes had lodging via the manager; Royal says in the 1950s a black band had to go abroad to be treated as men.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What about -- did Basie ride the bus?
Did he have a place to stay?
Sometimes he may and sometimes he may not.

That's right. Of course, the band manager or whoever was on the bus riding with us would go out and find a place for Basie to stay, because the band leader is always more acceptable than the side men. That's big time, you know? See, you don't ever get invited out to dinner until you've already got enough money in your pocket that you can pay for your own dinner. Then you're always invited out for dinner. But if you're hungry, nobody invites you to eat. They may give you a drink, but nobody invites you to have dinner.

That's what -- that was what? In the '60s (inaudible).
In middle and late '50s, before things got better. Yep, you had to go into another country to even be able to be treated like a man if you were in a black band.
